options.C: governments in these regions require most rural families to raise farm animals instead of growing crops
options.D: these regions are close to large cities whose residents buy fresh milk every day
options.E: heavy rainfall throughout the year makes it impossible to keep animals in one place

rationales.A: Incorrect. These regions have thin soils and little rain, which is why crop farming is difficult there.
rationales.B: Correct. Where rain is scarce and unpredictable, growing crops is risky. Herding livestock (camels, goats, sheep, cattle) and moving them with the seasons lets people use sparse grass and water spread across large areas, an extensive practice shaped by the physical environment.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The pattern reflects climate and environment, not government requirements.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nomadic herders typically live far from large city markets.
rationales.E: Incorrect. These regions are dry; heavy year-round rain is the opposite of their climate.

questions.explanation: In very dry places, crops often fail because there is not enough rain. But animals can eat the scattered grass. So herders move their animals from place to place with the seasons to find grass and water. The dry climate is the reason.

questions.stem: A farming region replaces many locally saved crop varieties with a few genetically modified varieties sold under patents. Which concern is most directly associated with this change?

options.A: Greater soil erosion caused by plowing steep slopes
options.B: Reduced food access caused by neighborhood grocery stores closing in nearby cities
options.C: Higher transport costs caused by longer routes to export markets
options.D: Reduced crop diversity and greater reliance on commercial seed suppliers
options.E: Higher soil salinity caused by irrigation in an arid climate

rationales.A: Incorrect. The change concerns seed varieties and patents, not cultivation of steep slopes.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The change described does not involve access to grocery stores.
rationales.C: Incorrect. No change in transportation routes or distance to markets is described.
rationales.D: Correct. Replacing many local varieties with a few commercial varieties reduces crop diversity, and patent restrictions can increase growers' dependence on seed suppliers. The AP course framework lists debates over reductions in biodiversity among the controversies surrounding biotechnology and GMOs.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Soil salinization is salt buildup, usually from irrigation in dry climates; no change in irrigation is described.

questions.explanation: Planting a few varieties instead of many means less crop diversity. Patents can also limit how farmers save or share seed, so they depend more on the companies that sell it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the fair trade movement in agriculture?

options.A: A trade agreement that removes all tariffs and quotas on goods traded between countries
options.B: A government program that pays farmers to leave some of their cropland unplanted
options.C: A movement that seeks better trading terms and labor and environmental standards for producers
options.D: A plan to replace imported food with food grown in each consumer's own backyard garden
options.E: A treaty that requires every country to grow its own coffee instead of importing it

rationales.A: Incorrect. That describes free trade, not fair trade.
rationales.B: Incorrect. That describes some conservation or price-support programs.
rationales.C: Correct. Fair trade programs seek better trading terms through standards, premiums, and, for many products, minimum prices. They also set labor and environmental standards. The AP course framework lists fair trade among movements influencing food production and consumption.
rationales.D: Incorrect. That is closer to urban farming or the local-food movement.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Coffee grows only in suitable tropical climates; no such treaty exists.

questions.explanation: Fair trade programs try to give farmers better deals and to protect workers and the environment. For many products, such as coffee and cocoa, buyers must pay at least a minimum price plus an extra amount that farmer groups can spend on their communities.

questions.stem: Property boundaries in parts of the original thirteen U.S. colonies were described using natural features such as streams, large trees, and stones, producing irregularly shaped parcels. This survey method is called

options.A: township and range
options.B: the long-lot system
options.C: the open-field system
options.D: metes and bounds
options.E: enclosure

rationales.A: Incorrect. Township and range uses a rectangular grid of squares, not natural landmarks.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Long lots are narrow strips running back from a river, used in French settlement areas.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Enclosure is the British consolidation of open fields and common land, not a surveying method.
rationales.D: Correct. Metes and bounds describes boundaries by distances and directions between landmarks such as streams, trees, and stones, producing irregular parcels. It was widely used in the colonial East and came from British practice.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The open-field system was the medieval European pattern of scattered strips farmed around a village, not a way of describing property lines.

questions.explanation: Metes and bounds uses landmarks to mark property lines: "from the big oak tree, 200 feet to the creek, then along the creek to the stone wall." Because nature is not in straight lines, the parcels have odd, irregular shapes. You see it in the eastern U.S.
